We use five public binary-classification tables, chosen to span the number of players $d$: German Credit ($d=20$, 1000 rows), ACS Employment ($d=16$) and ACS Income ($d=10$) from the 2018 one-year person file for California \citep{ding2021}, Pima Indians Diabetes ($d=8$) and Give Me Some Credit ($d=10$).

We run (i) the unchanged \texttt{KernelExplainer} of the \texttt{shap} package (version 0.51.0) with its default sampling, with \texttt{l1\_reg} set to \texttt{False}, \texttt{"auto"} (the default) and \texttt{"num\_features(10)"}; (ii) unbiased paired Kernel SHAP \citep{covert2021}; and (iii) antithetic permutation sampling \citep{mitchell2022}.

For a tabular model, a SHAP value per feature is estimated once by a randomised, budget-limited algorithm, and the reader draws a conclusion from that single result: which feature mattered most, which three mattered, whether a feature pushed the score up or down.
The literature on Shapley estimators measures how close an estimate is to the exact Shapley value, usually in $\ell_2$, averaged over instances and at chosen budgets \citep{lundberg2017,covert2021,mitchell2022,musco2025}.
A small average error does not say that a particular run returns the conclusion the exact values would give: when two features are nearly tied, a tiny error swaps them.
Our question is therefore how far one randomised, budget-limited SHAP run can be treated as a reliable basis for a prediction, where the prediction is the conclusion a reader draws.

We answer it for the unchanged \texttt{shap} Kernel explainer and two sampled alternatives, on four model classes and five public tabular datasets, with the value function fixed so that the randomness of the explainer is not confused with the choice of what is explained (Section~\ref{sec:setting}).
The reference is the exact Shapley value of that value function, obtained by enumerating all coalitions once per instance, so every run is scored against the quantity it estimates.
For each instance we measure the probability $P_c$ that a run returns the exact top-$k$ set, a tolerance-aware version that forgives swaps across an exact near tie, and the agreement of two runs, and we summarise a dataset--model cell by the share of its instances for which one run is correct with probability at least $0.9$.
We compare the explainer's own noise with the noise from drawing another background and from retraining the model, and we test whether a certificate computed from one run is a better check than running twice.

\paragraph{Results.}
In these cells the answer is conditional, and the condition is explicit.
(i)~At the \texttt{shap} default budget, one run returns the exact top-3 set with probability at least $0.9$ for $0.90$--$1.00$ of the instances of each cell on the two datasets with $d\ge16$, and for every instance once swaps across near ties are forgiven; at half of all coalitions on the three smaller datasets the strict share is $0.79$--$1.00$ (Section~\ref{sec:headline}).
(ii)~The failures are the instances whose third and fourth features are nearly tied, and the mean correlation with the exact values, at least $0.97$ at every budget of $3d$ or more, would not have warned of them (Section~\ref{sec:margin}).
(iii)~Below that, a run cannot be treated as reliable: at three to four times as many coalitions as features the tolerance-aware share is $0.65$--$0.97$ for the non-linear models of the two larger datasets, and near zero at twice as many; the budget a margin requires grows roughly as $g^{-1.5}$ to $g^{-2}$ in the margin $g$, neither confirming nor refuting the $g^{-2}$ of a Gaussian argument (Section~\ref{sec:budget}).
(iv)~With a background of $50$ random rows, two runs of the explainer agree on the top-3 set far more often ($0.91$--$0.99$ at the reference budget) than two exactly explained backgrounds ($0.27$--$0.69$) or two retrained models (three definitions, wider and less certain); this is a statement about the \texttt{shap} default at $B=50$: the paired Kernel estimator, noisier at the same budget, does not show it in general, and part of the background's effect is its finite size (Section~\ref{sec:floors}).
(v)~A certificate from one run is not a clear improvement over running twice (Section~\ref{sec:cert}).

\paragraph{Scope.}
The headline rests on two populations and one trained model per model class, with one seed and a marginal value function with $B=50$ random background rows; its intervals resample instances and do not contain training or background variance.
Five datasets are five observations of the setting, so the findings are per dataset and carry no dataset-level interval.
